study.title: There is surely a God who judges the earth.
study.intro: Eleven verses confront corrupt rulers whose justice is violence, compare them to a deaf cobra, ask God to break their power with a string of vivid images, and end with confidence that God judges the earth.
study.context: The heading names David and the tune 'Do Not Destroy.' Verse 1 addresses 'rulers' (the Hebrew may also mean 'gods' or 'mighty ones'), probably human judges or powers responsible for justice; compare Psalm 82. Verses 1–5 indict them for injustice and violence, verses 6–9 ask God to break their power with images of shattered teeth, runoff water, blunted arrows, a dissolving slug, a stillborn child and thorns swept away, and verses 10–11 picture the vindication of the righteous. This is among the harshest psalms. The notes read it as a cry from victims of corrupt justice who hand judgment to God, not as permission for violence, and treat the image in verse 10 of washing feet in blood as ancient battlefield hyperbole for complete vindication. The stillborn image in verse 8 is handled with care, as it may touch readers who have lost a child; it describes the wicked's power never coming to life, not a judgment on any child. The Scripture is loaded unchanged from the bundled BSB, including the heading.
study.peopleNote: David is named in the heading, with the tune 'Do Not Destroy.' His profile covers his life under the unjust rule of Saul. No other person is named. Planned paintings avoid gore entirely and show courtrooms, a cobra, streams, blunted arrows, thorns and light; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: Do you speak justly?
verses.heading: Confronting the rulers
verses.meaning: The heading names David and the tune 'Do Not Destroy.' David confronts rulers directly. The word translated 'rulers' can mean gods or mighty ones, probably the human judges and powers who were supposed to uphold justice. He asks whether they really judge fairly. The question is sharp and ironic. The answer, given in verse 2, is no. The psalm begins as an indictment of corrupt authority.
verses.context: Psalm 82:1–4 pictures God judging the 'gods' who defend the unjust, and Amos 5:7 condemns those who turn justice into bitterness. Deuteronomy 16:18–20 commands judges to judge fairly.
explore: O rulers
The word may mean gods or mighty ones. It refers to those with power to judge.
Speak justly
The question is ironic. The rulers do not judge fairly.
verses.reflect: Where do you see injustice in those who hold power? How could you pray for justice?
verses.alt: Empty judges' seats sit in a shadowed gate court with a tilted scale.

verses.title: You devise injustice
verses.heading: Hearts and hands corrupt
verses.meaning: No, in your hearts you devise injustice; with your hands you mete out violence on the earth. The answer comes. The rulers plan injustice in their hearts. With their hands they weigh out violence instead of justice. The image of weighing recalls scales of justice turned into scales of violence. Inner plans lead to outer harm. The corruption runs from heart to hand.
verses.context: Micah 2:1 warns those who plot evil on their beds, and Isaiah 10:1–2 condemns those who enact unjust laws to rob the poor. Psalm 58:2 describes justice turned to violence.
explore: In your hearts
The injustice is planned in advance. It starts inside before it reaches the courts.
Mete out violence
They weigh out harm. Justice is replaced by violence.
verses.reflect: How do hidden thoughts lead to outward actions in your life?
verses.alt: A judge's scale weighs a dagger instead of silver.

verses.title: Astray from birth
verses.heading: Long-standing deceit
verses.meaning: The wicked are estranged from the womb; the liars go astray from birth. David describes the rulers and their kind as wayward from the beginning. The language is poetic exaggeration, emphasizing how deeply rooted their lying is. It echoes Psalm 51:5 but with a different purpose: here it describes those who persist in evil, not a confession. The verse names a settled pattern of falsehood.
verses.context: Psalm 51:5 confesses sin from birth, and Isaiah 48:8 says, 'You have been called a rebel from birth.' Psalm 58:3 describes a deeply rooted habit of lying.
explore: Estranged from the womb
Poetic exaggeration. It shows how deep their lies go.
Go astray
They wander from truth. Their path is crooked from the start.
verses.reflect: Are there long-standing habits in your life that need God's correction?
verses.alt: A crooked path veers away from a straight road across a plain.

verses.title: Venom of a snake
verses.heading: Poisonous deceit
verses.meaning: Their venom is like the venom of a snake, like a cobra that shuts its ears. The rulers' words are compared to snake venom. They poison whoever they touch. Then the image shifts to a cobra that stops its ears. Snake charmers played music to calm cobras, but this one refuses to listen. The rulers cannot be reasoned with. They shut out every appeal to justice.
verses.context: Psalm 140:3 says, 'The venom of vipers is on their lips,' and Romans 3:13 quotes that line. Jeremiah 8:17 mentions snakes that cannot be charmed.
explore: Venom
Their words poison like venom. Injustice spreads harm to everyone it touches.
Shuts its ears
They refuse to listen. No appeal to justice or mercy reaches them.
verses.reflect: Are there areas where you have closed your ears to God's correction?
verses.alt: A cobra rises with its hood spread in dry rocky ground.

verses.title: Refusing the charmer
verses.heading: No listening to wisdom
verses.meaning: Refusing to hear the tune of the charmer who skillfully weaves his spell. The image of the deaf cobra continues. Even the most skilled charmer cannot reach it. The rulers are like that. No wise counsel, no prophetic warning, no plea for justice can soften them. The verse emphasizes their hardness. It prepares for David's appeal to God, since human persuasion has failed.
verses.context: Ecclesiastes 10:11 says, 'If the snake bites before it is charmed, there is no profit for the charmer,' and Zechariah 7:11–12 describes people who stopped their ears and made their hearts like flint. Psalm 58:5 describes the same stubbornness.
explore: Refusing to hear
No skill or wisdom reaches them. They resist every appeal to do right.
Skillfully weaves
Even the best persuasion fails. They are beyond human correction.
verses.reflect: Who has tried to give you wise counsel that you resisted?
verses.alt: A flute lies abandoned beside a basket as a snake slides away.

verses.title: Break the fangs
verses.heading: Asking God to disarm the oppressors
verses.meaning: O God, shatter their teeth in their mouths; O LORD, tear out the fangs of the lions. David turns to God and asks Him to break the power of the corrupt rulers. The images are violent, but their meaning is disarming: a lion without teeth cannot devour. The prayer asks God to stop their ability to harm, not for David to harm them. It comes from the perspective of victims who have no other recourse.
verses.context: Psalm 3:7 says, 'You break the teeth of the wicked,' and Job 29:17 describes Job breaking the fangs of the wicked to rescue the victim. Psalm 58:6 asks God to stop oppressors from devouring.
explore: Shatter their teeth
The image means removing their power to harm. It asks God to disarm them.
Fangs of the lions
The corrupt rulers are like lions. They devour the weak who come before them.
verses.reflect: Where do you long for God to stop someone's power to harm others?
verses.alt: An old toothless lion rests harmless beside a sheepfold.

verses.title: Like water that runs off
verses.heading: Vanishing and blunted
verses.meaning: May they vanish like water that runs off; when they draw the bow, may their arrows be blunted. David asks that the oppressors disappear like water poured on dry ground that soaks away. When they try to shoot, may their arrows fall harmless. The images express a hope that their power will fail and fade. Water draining away is a quiet picture of something gone and not returning.
verses.context: 2 Samuel 14:14 says, 'Like water poured out on the ground, which cannot be recovered,' and Psalm 64:7 says God will shoot the wicked with arrows. Psalm 58:7 asks for their weapons to fail.
explore: Vanish like water
Their power will drain away like water into sand. It will not last.
Arrows blunted
Their attacks will fail. Arrows meant to wound will fall harmless.
verses.reflect: What threats in your life do you long to see fade like water into sand?
verses.alt: Water drains away into cracked desert sand beside blunted arrows.

verses.title: Never see the sun
verses.heading: Images of power that never lives
verses.meaning: Like a slug that dissolves in its slime, like a woman's stillborn child, may they never see the sun. Two images follow. A slug seemed to melt away as it moved. A stillborn child never sees daylight. These images, painful to modern readers, express the hope that the rulers' power will never come to life. For readers who have lost a child, this verse may be hard; it is not a statement about any child's worth, but a picture of something that never reaches the light. The image underlines how completely their schemes will fail.
verses.context: Job 3:16 says, 'Why was I not hidden like a stillborn child, like an infant who never sees daylight?' and Ecclesiastes 6:3–5 uses the same picture of something that never saw the sun. Psalm 58:8 applies it to the wicked rulers' power, not to any child.
explore: A slug dissolving
The image is of something wasting away. The rulers' power will melt.
Never see the sun
The hope is that their schemes never reach the light. It is about their power, not any child.
verses.reflect: If this verse touches your own grief, how could you bring that grief to God honestly?
verses.alt: A snail trail fades on a rock as dawn light falls nearby.

verses.title: Thorns swept away
verses.heading: Sudden judgment
verses.meaning: Before your pots can feel the burning thorns, whether green or dry, He will sweep them away. The image is of a cooking fire. Thorns burned quickly beneath pots. Before the heat even reaches the pot, the wind sweeps everything away. The point is speed. God's judgment will come before the wicked expect it. The Hebrew is difficult, but the sense of sudden removal is clear.
verses.context: Ecclesiastes 7:6 compares a fool's laughter to crackling thorns under a pot, and Proverbs 10:25 says, 'When the whirlwind passes, the wicked are no more.' Psalm 58:9 pictures sudden judgment.
explore: Burning thorns
Thorns burned fast. The image is of something quick.
Sweep them away
God's judgment comes suddenly. It removes the wicked quickly.
verses.reflect: How does knowing God's justice can come suddenly change how you view injustice?
verses.alt: A gust of wind scatters burning thorns from beneath a cooking pot.

verses.title: The righteous rejoice
verses.heading: Vindication pictured
verses.meaning: The righteous will rejoice when they see they are avenged; they will wash their feet in the blood of the wicked. This verse pictures victims seeing justice done. 'Washing feet in blood' is ancient battlefield hyperbole for complete victory, the sort of language found in war poetry. It is not a description of literal cruelty or a call to violence. The rejoicing is relief that oppression has ended. The New Testament asks believers to love enemies and leave vengeance to God (Romans 12:19–21).
verses.context: Psalm 68:23 uses similar battlefield language, and Revelation 19:1–2 rejoices that God has judged justly. Proverbs 24:17 warns, 'Do not gloat when your enemy falls,' and Romans 12:19–21 leaves vengeance to God.
explore: Rejoice when avenged
Victims finally see justice done. Their relief after oppression is real.
Wash their feet
The image is battlefield hyperbole. It means complete vindication, not cruelty.
verses.reflect: How do you feel when justice is done for victims? How do you guard your heart against cruelty?
verses.alt: Freed captives walk out of an open prison gate into sunlight.

verses.title: A God who judges the earth
verses.heading: The final confession
verses.meaning: Then men will say, 'There is surely a reward for the righteous! There is surely a God who judges the earth!' The psalm ends with its point. When God acts, people will see that righteousness is not in vain. There is a God who judges. The corrupt rulers of verse 1 did not judge justly, but God does. The psalm moves from false judges to the true Judge. This is its deepest hope.
verses.context: Genesis 18:25 asks, 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?' and Psalm 96:13 says the LORD comes to judge the earth. Psalm 58:11 answers verse 1's question with God's justice.
explore: A reward for the righteous
Faithfulness is not in vain. God sees and rewards it.
A God who judges
God is the true Judge, unlike the corrupt rulers. He will set things right.
verses.reflect: How does knowing there is a God who judges the earth help you persist in doing right?
verses.alt: Sunlight floods an empty court of justice through high windows.
